one_liner: Rust crates that bake immutable perfect-hash maps and sets into the binary at compile time, removing runtime HashMap construction.
what_it_does: rust-phf builds static, read-only Map, Set, OrderedMap and OrderedSet values at compile time. You make them with the phf_map!/phf_set! proc macros, or with phf_codegen in a build.rs that writes Rust source, for example from a JSON file. The result is a `static` with no runtime initializer and no heap allocation, so it replaces the lazy_static/OnceLock + HashMap::insert pattern for fixed tables. Lookups work much like HashMap (get, contains_key, get_entry, get_key, Index, iteration in a fixed order), but there is no insert or remove, and keys must be PhfHash types: str/String, byte strings, integers, char, bool, arrays, tuples of up to 12 elements, and UniCase/UncasedStr behind features.
how_it_is_fast: The gain is at startup. The table is solved at build time and stored as `&'static` slices in the binary's read-only data, so nothing is allocated or hashed when the program loads. The default layout is CHD (Compress, Hash, Displace; Belazzougui, Botelho and Dietzfelbinger, ESA 2009): a SipHash-1-3 128-bit hash of the key is split into g, f1 and f2. g picks a bucket (about 3 keys per bucket), and that bucket's stored displacement pair (d1, d2) gives the slot (d2 + f1*d1 + f2) mod n. One key comparison then decides hit or miss. The experimental `ptrhash` feature switches to a PtrHash-style layout (8-bit pilot per bucket, Lemire multiply-shift range reduction, a remap array for the ~1% spare slots), which the maintainer measured at 26-35% higher lookup throughput than CHD. Neither layout is inherently faster per lookup than std HashMap, because the SipHash cost dominates.
when_to_use: Fixed lookup tables known at build time (keywords, MIME types, HTML entities, charset or Unicode names) that you now fill into a HashMap in lazy_static/OnceLock: init cost and heap allocation drop to zero. In conduit-mime-types, Types::new() went from a reported 300 ms to 3 ns.

Short-lived processes, CLIs, cold-start-sensitive services, and no_std/embedded targets, where you cannot or do not want to run initializers or allocate. The runtime crate builds with default-features = false.

Tables generated from data files at build time via phf_codegen in build.rs. Generation cost is paid by the build: the maintainer measured 6.2 ms to solve 10,000 keys with CHD, and hashify's measurements show about 3 s of added build time at 100k keys and 42 s at 1M.

You need a first-class static map value: iterate entries or keys in fixed order, use OrderedMap/OrderedSet for index order, call get_key for interning, serialize via serde, or key by case-insensitive strings through unicase/uncased.
Cross-compiled builds: PhfHash is designed to be architecture-independent (portable SipHasher, fixed-endian integer hashing), so tables generated on the host are valid on the target.
when_not_to_use: Hot-path lookups where per-lookup latency matters. Every lookup runs SipHash-1-3 (128-bit) plus a modulo. A 2023 users.rust-lang.org Criterion test at 100 string keys had phf::Map about 10% slower than std HashMap (8.61-8.79 us vs 7.74-7.86 us per 229-lookup batch). A 2025 rust-phf issue (#349) says the crate is 'almost always slower than hashmap' at lookup.

Small keyword sets, where a plain `match` wins. hashify's README (Apple M5 Max, Rust 1.98) measures match hits at 1.3-2.8 ns vs 8.6-9.7 ns for phf at 9-149 keys. phf only beats match on its 2,125-key set (9.1 ns vs 25.1 ns).
Keys or values not known when you build, or tables that must change at runtime. Maps are immutable; to add or remove a key you regenerate and recompile.

Key types outside PhfHash (arbitrary structs, enum keys: open issue #196), or macro keys computed by const expressions (open issue #188, blocked on const traits). Every phf_map! key must use the same literal shape.
Huge phf_map! invocations in a crate you rebuild often: the proc macro reruns on every compile of that crate. Put big tables in their own crate or generate them with phf_codegen.

integration.form: crate (phf runtime + phf_macros proc-macro via the `macros` feature, or phf_codegen as a build-dependency)
integration.dependencies: phf -> phf_shared -> siphasher; optional serde, unicase, uncased; `macros` adds phf_macros (syn, quote, proc-macro2, phf_generator -> fastrand); phf_codegen build-dep pulls phf_generator + phf_shared (quote/proc-macro2 optional)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 (MSRV, edition 2024) for phf 0.14; the in-repo phf-vs-HashMap lookup bench needs nightly (#[bench])
integration.platforms: Any Rust target including no_std (default-features = false); hashing is made endian/pointer-width independent for cross-compiling; CI runs only on ubuntu-latest (1.85, stable, nightly)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented explicitly. A Map holds only a u64 seed and `&'static` slices, lookups take &self, and a Rust `static` must be Sync, so concurrent reads need no locks.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — read API mirrors HashMap (get/contains_key/Index/iteration) with borrowed lookup keys via PhfEq, but the map must be declared as a static through phf_map! or build.rs codegen, has no insert/remove, and only supports PhfHash key types

gotchas: phf_map! syntax is picky: integer literals in the first key must carry suffixes (0u32), and all keys must share the first key's expression type. OR patterns (`"+" | "add" => ...`) work in the macros but not in phf_codegen. Per-entry #[cfg] is handled by a decl-macro resolver since 0.14, after issue #356's overflow panic with many cfg'd entries, but a request for cfg support (#449) is still open, so test your case.

The `ptrhash` feature changes the Map struct's fields (pilots/remap instead of disps). It must be enabled on both the generator (phf_codegen/phf_macros) and the runtime phf crate. Because Cargo unifies features, one build uses one layout.

phf_codegen writes each value string verbatim as Rust source (you write "\"addition\"" for a &str value). build() panics on duplicate keys. The docs warn that 500+ chained .entry() calls overflow the compiler's stack; loop instead. The generated struct literal fills doc-hidden fields that 'are subject to change at any time', so keep phf and phf_codegen on the same version.
`MAP[key]` (Index) panics with 'invalid key' on a miss. Use get() on untrusted input.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: hashify, the only other Rust entry, looks up keys 4.1-12.6x faster than phf's default layout on its own Apple M5 Max benchmark. Its macros, though, return a lookup result in expression position over byte-slice keys and do not document iteration. Pick rust-phf when you need a named static Map/Set you can iterate, serialize or intern through, tuple keys, Unicode case-insensitive keys, or build.rs generation from data files. For C++ code use frozen, mph or constexpr-phf instead, since rust-phf is Rust-only.
verified_claims_summary: The only rust-phf-specific number is first-party, from conduit-mime-types PR #18 (Tobias Bieniek, merged 2021-10-11). Replacing runtime insertion of bundled MIME data into two std::collections::HashMaps with two phf_codegen-generated static maps made Types::new() run in '3ns instead of 300ms'. No hardware, compiler or methodology is given, and the Criterion bench was deleted in the same PR. It measures initialization moved to build time, not lookup speed; the Mainmatter post's ~80% figure belongs to the earlier non-phf codegen step (PR #17).
status_note: Actively maintained: 0.14.0 released 2026-06-21 and commits through 2026-09-17. MIT-licensed and very widely used (~562M crates.io downloads, 1,176 reverse dependencies). The faster ptrhash layout is still marked experimental, and issue #458 proposes further tuning.
